paras: The Hahira near-riot of 1903 was an armed standoff between about twenty white men and as many Black men at Hahira, Lowndes County, Georgia, on the night of December 23, 1903. The sheriff asked Governor Terrell for troops, and the crowds dispersed once the request became known, with no deaths reported. Wire services carried it as a "race riot" narrowly averted, and papers from Texas to Minnesota printed the story.

According to the Valdosta correspondent of the Savannah Morning News, a crowd of young white men held a turkey shooting that afternoon and drank "a good deal of liquor" around supper time. Some of them then entered a "negro restaurant" and "offended negroes who were there," who resented it; both sides armed, and for several hours the two groups stood "in battle array," with several "knock-down and drag-out fights." A shorter wire from Hahira said only that the dispute was "stated" to have arisen "over the killing of a turkey."

Squire Lawson of Hahira telegraphed Sheriff Passmore for military help, and the sheriff wired the governor, who ordered the Valdosta Videttes to report to him. The trouble subsided when the two factions learned that the company was ready, and the sheriff and a deputy who reached Hahira before daybreak found the town quiet.
On December 24 a young white man named Pike Vickers, called "one of the rioters," was arrested and released on a $150 bond. No report of further proceedings against him was found.

The first word, telegraphed from Atlanta on the night of December 23, named no race and said that "several men had defied local officers" and were running Hahira "to their own liking." A Macon dispatch the same night called it "a race riot," though Valdosta was "not informed of the facts," and the Raleigh News and Observer headed it "A Race Riot Is On." The next day's wire, run by the Washington Evening Star, the Birmingham Age-Herald and the San Antonio Daily Light, described white men "celebrating Christmas" and "some negroes" and the San Antonio paper headed it "Riot over a Turkey."

Only the Savannah Morning News printed a local account, headed "Military Not Needed," which said the young white men "were really responsible for the row, though they were only having fun when the trouble started." A week later, papers in Minnesota and South Carolina were still running an Atlanta item calling the information "meager." All of the coverage found came from white daily and weekly papers; no account of it was found in the Black press.

The papers spelled the sheriff's name as Passmore, Passamore and Bassamore, while the first Atlanta report called him Patterson. The Atlanta dispatch said the governor "at once" wired the Videttes, but the Valdosta report said the sheriff received no reply until after breakfast the next morning.

bases: The papers describe an armed standoff of about twenty white men and as many Black men with fistfights, set off when young white men offended Black patrons of a restaurant, that ended without reported deaths or injuries once troops were requested (A6, A2, A4).

Separate Atlanta/Macon dispatches (A1, A5), a Hahira wire (A2, A3, A4) and a Valdosta correspondent (A6) agree that a riot was feared at Hahira on the night of Dec. 23 and that the sheriff asked for troops.

accounts.label: First Atlanta/Macon dispatches
accounts.gist: The sheriff wired for troops to suppress a riot at Hahira where 'several men' had defied local officers; Valdosta had no details, though Macon heard it was a race riot.

accounts.label: Hahira wire
accounts.gist: A race riot between white men celebrating Christmas and some Black men was narrowly averted; the men dispersed once the call for troops was known; the trouble was said to have begun over the killing of a turkey.

accounts.label: Valdosta correspondent
accounts.gist: After a turkey shoot and drinking, young white men entered a Black restaurant and offended the patrons; about twenty armed men on each side faced off for hours with several fights; the young white men were 'really responsible'.

framing.detail: Headlines spoke of 'Rioting at Hahira' and troops called out, with no race stated in the first Atlanta item.
Out-of-state papers ran the short Hahira wire as 'Race Riot Averted', 'Riot Averted' or 'Riot over a Turkey'.
The Savannah Morning News's Valdosta report, 'Military Not Needed', placed the blame on the young white men while saying they were 'only having fun'.
A late Atlanta wire calling the information 'meager' ran in Minnesota and South Carolina a week later.

conflicts.note: The Valdosta account (A6) is the most detailed and nearest; the Atlanta item (A1) was sent before any details reached Valdosta.
Passmore appears in the local Valdosta report; the others look like transmission or OCR variants.

conflicts.note: Unresolved; both agree the Videttes were readied.
